| Small/hyperdynamic LV + positive dynamic flow response | Look for true volume loss/vasodilation; give a small measured fluid bolus only if clinically indicated and tolerated, and use vasopressor if vascular tone remains the dominant problem. |
| Severe LV systolic dysfunction / new regional abnormality | Avoid repeated empirical fluid; support coronary perfusion, evaluate ischaemia/afterload/rhythm and consider inotropy or specialist escalation where appropriate. |
| Dilated failing RV / septal flattening | Maintain systemic pressure/RV perfusion, correct hypoxaemia/hypercapnia/acidosis, reduce pulmonary vascular load and treat the cause such as PE; avoid RV overdistension. |
| Tamponade physiology | Prioritise urgent drainage and preserve venous return/contractility until relieved. |
| No clear cardiac mechanism | Reassess haemorrhage, anaesthetic depth, tension pneumothorax, equipment and distributive causes; do not force an echo diagnosis. |

## 6. Overall evaluation

In an unstable anaesthetised patient, TTE is particularly valuable when the cause is uncertain and a rapid distinction between preload, LV, RV, obstructive and vasodilatory physiology will alter therapy. Its usefulness falls when windows/access are poor or when the operator cannot obtain/interpret a focused study reliably.

**Examiner lens:** The 2025.2 report said many candidates lost marks by giving generic uses or discussing TOE/preoperative echo. Strong answers stayed specific to intraoperative TTE, used it to distinguish shock states and assess response to therapy, and explicitly evaluated patient, surgical, training and equipment limitations.

items.title: 11. Point-of-care ultrasound in undifferentiated shock
items.q: Discuss the role of point-of-care ultrasound in the management of a patient with undifferentiated shock in the intensive care unit.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Point-of-care ultrasound in shock" (BJA Educ 2026): POCUS rapidly diagnoses the cause of shock, guides therapy and its response, guides emergency interventions and allows serial reassessment.

## Role

Shock types: distributive, hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, obstructive. Examination alone is unreliable. POCUS is **rapid, non-invasive and repeatable**, needs no transfer or radiation, and guidelines recommend assessment of all patients with hypoperfusion.

## Findings by shock type

| Type | Ultrasound findings |
|---|---|
| **Hypovolaemic** | Small, hyperdynamic, "kissing" LV; collapsing IVC; flat lungs |
| **Distributive** | Hyperdynamic LV (or septic cardiomyopathy); variable IVC |
| **Cardiogenic** | Poor LV function and dilated LV; B-lines; plethoric IVC |
| **Obstructive** | Tamponade (effusion, RA or RV collapse); pulmonary embolus (dilated RV, septal flattening, McConnell sign); tension pneumothorax (absent sliding, lung point) |

Also look at lungs (B-lines, effusion), abdomen (free fluid, aortic aneurysm) and veins (DVT).

## Guiding therapy

Fluid challenge response (VTI, IVC), inotrope or vasopressor choice (LV function, SVR), and early intervention: **pericardiocentesis, pleural drainage** and line placement under ultrasound. Serial scans show the response and prompt changes.

## Limitations

- Operator training and experience; risk of misinterpretation.
- Windows (ventilation, obesity, dressings, subcutaneous emphysema), intermittent nature.
- Overlapping or mixed shock states; static IVC measures are unreliable on positive pressure.
- Not a substitute for clinical assessment; formal echo may be needed.

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes the four shock types and the role of POCUS in diagnosing them
- Gives findings in each shock type
- Describes use to guide fluid, vasopressors and inotropes
- Mentions procedural guidance (pericardiocentesis, drainage)
- Mentions serial reassessment
- States limitations (training, windows, mixed states)

items.title: 12. TOE in non-cardiac surgery: indications, contraindications, complications
items.q: Discuss the indications, contraindications and complications of transoesophageal echocardiography for intraoperative haemodynamic monitoring in non-cardiac surgery.
items.a:
## Indications

- **Unexplained or persistent haemodynamic instability** when TTE fails or surgery blocks windows.
- Intraoperative monitoring in high-risk surgery: liver and lung transplantation, major vascular surgery, thoracoabdominal aneurysm, trauma, patients with known ventricular dysfunction or valve disease.
- Diagnosis of embolism (air, thrombus, fat), tamponade, acute LV or RV failure, ischaemia (new regional wall motion abnormality) and aortic dissection.
- Guiding volume and inotropic or vasopressor therapy; confirming placement of lines, cannulae and devices.

## Advantages

Continuous monitoring, excellent views not limited by the surgical field, quantitative Doppler and 3D, and rapid diagnosis in unstable patients.

## Contraindications

**Absolute:** oesophageal stricture, tumour, perforation, diverticulum, recent oesophageal surgery, active upper GI bleeding.
**Relative:** varices or severe coagulopathy, cervical spine instability or limited neck movement, hiatus hernia, previous radiotherapy to the chest or neck, dysphagia, atlantoaxial disease.

## Complications

- **Oesophageal injury** (mucosal damage, haematoma, perforation; rare but serious), dental or lip injury, bleeding.
- Hoarseness, vocal cord and recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, throat pain.
- Haemodynamic effects (hypotension, arrhythmia), airway displacement or endotracheal tube dislodgement, and compression of the left atrium or vessels in children.
- Prolonged use: heat injury to the oesophagus; infection control.

## Practical points

Check the swallowing history, gentle insertion under direct view or with a laryngoscope, avoid force, freeze and withdraw the probe when not in use, and use the limited standard views (mid-oesophageal four-chamber, transgastric short-axis, long-axis, bicaval). Training is required (ANZCA PS46).

## Self-marking checklist

- Gives indications for intraoperative monitoring and diagnosis
- States advantages over TTE
- Lists absolute and relative contraindications
- Lists complications with oesophageal injury highlighted
- Gives practical safety points
- Mentions training requirement

items.title: 13. TTE versus TOE versus PAC in complex haemodynamic instability
items.q: Compare TTE, TOE and a pulmonary artery catheter for the assessment of complex perioperative haemodynamic instability. Give examples of when you would favour each.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would compare the three by the type of information they provide, invasiveness, continuity, access and operator dependence. They are complementary rather than mutually exclusive: echo is strongest for anatomy and mechanism, while a PAC is strongest for continuous pulmonary pressure/flow/SvO₂ data in selected complex physiology.

## 1. Comparison

| Feature | TTE | TOE | PAC |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main information | Ventricular/pericardial/valve anatomy + flow; lung POCUS adjunct. | High-quality cardiac/valve/aortic imaging when TTE access poor. | RA/PA pressures, PAOP, CO/CI, SvO₂ and derived SVR/PVR. |
| Invasiveness | Non-invasive. | Semi-invasive oesophageal probe. | Invasive central/right-heart catheter. |
| Continuity | Intermittent. | Can be repeated/near-continuous intraoperatively. | Continuous pressure and often CO/SvO₂ trend. |
| Major strengths | Rapid shock phenotype; treatment response; no vascular instrumentation. | Excellent intraoperative windows and structural detail. | Serial pulmonary haemodynamics and flow/oxygen-balance data. |
| Limitations | Windows/access/operator dependent. | Oesophageal contraindications/injury, training, anaesthesia dependence. | Serious complications and measurement assumptions; no routine survival benefit. |

## 2. When I would favour TTE
- Initial unexplained hypotension/shock when windows are accessible and I need a rapid mechanism diagnosis.
- Serial bedside reassessment where a non-invasive study can answer the question.
- When lung POCUS and cardiac findings together are useful.

## 3. When I would favour TOE
- Intraoperative instability with poor TTE access due to drapes/position/open surgery.
- Need for detailed valve, aortic or surgical structural assessment in an appropriately trained setting.
- Continuous/repeated cardiac imaging during major cardiac/vascular surgery.

## 4. When I would favour a PAC
- Severe pulmonary hypertension or RV failure where serial PA pressure, PVR, CO and SvO₂ directly guide therapy.
- Selected complex cardiac surgery/mechanical support or refractory mixed shock when continuous invasive data add information that echo cannot provide continuously.

## 5. Overall judgement

I would usually start with the least invasive tool that can answer the clinical question. Echo often comes early because it identifies mechanism. A PAC is justified when its unique continuous pulmonary haemodynamic/flow information is actionable and outweighs procedural risk.

items.title: 14. Applying ANZCA monitoring standards in a remote anaesthetising location
items.q: You are asked to provide general anaesthesia for an interventional radiology procedure in a remote suite. Outline how you would determine whether the location, staffing, equipment and monitoring are adequate, and what monitoring you would apply.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would start with the principle that the standard of patient safety does not fall because the procedure occurs outside theatre. I would assess the patient/procedure risk and the environment against PS55, apply PG18 clinical observation and physiological monitoring, then add case-specific monitoring and ensure rescue/recovery/transfer capability.

## 1. Decide whether this patient/procedure belongs in this location
- Patient factors: airway, comorbidity, haemodynamic/respiratory reserve, obesity/OSA, anticipated blood loss, need for advanced monitoring or postoperative support.
- Procedure factors: duration, position, limited access to the airway/patient, contrast/radiation, bleeding/vascular complications and whether the procedure itself may cause abrupt instability.
- Environment: physical space, lighting, electrical/gas supply, access to the patient, infection control, ability to evacuate/transfer and proximity of emergency support.

## 2. Staffing and rescue capability
- Appropriately trained anaesthetist and assistant; clear roles and communication with procedural staff.
- Immediate access to additional skilled help, resuscitation/defibrillation, difficult-airway equipment and emergency drugs.
- A safe recovery plan with appropriately trained staff, monitoring and transfer pathway to PACU/ICU.

## 3. Monitoring

PG18 places continuous clinical observation and vigilance alongside electronic monitoring. I would use the standard monitoring required for the anaesthetic technique — oxygenation, ventilation/capnography as appropriate, circulation with ECG/pulse and BP, inspired gases/agent where relevant — and make sure alarms are audible and enabled. BP intervals should shorten with instability; I would not accept a remote setup where the patient cannot be observed or alarms cannot be heard.

## 4. Add monitoring for specific risk

| Risk | Additional monitoring / preparation |
|---|---|
| Expected rapid BP change / vasoactive infusion | Arterial catheter; infusion pumps and secure access. |
| Major bleeding | Arterial line, serial Hb/coagulation as indicated, rapid-infusion/warming capability, blood access. |
| Severe cardiac disease | Echo/TOE or advanced haemodynamic monitoring where results will change management. |
| Long procedure / temperature risk | Temperature monitoring and active warming. |

## 5. If the suite cannot support the plan

I would change the anaesthetic technique, bring additional equipment/personnel, or move the procedure to a location that can safely support the patient. “Remote” is not a justification for lowering the standard.

items.title: 15. Choosing monitoring for a high-risk anaesthetic
items.q: A patient with severe pulmonary hypertension and RV dysfunction requires urgent non-cardiac surgery. Justify the monitoring you would use and explain what each addition would change in your management.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would justify each monitor against a specific threat: acute RV failure, systemic hypotension reducing RV coronary perfusion, arrhythmia, hypoxaemia/hypercapnia and abrupt changes in pulmonary vascular resistance. I would use standard monitoring plus beat-to-beat pressure, direct assessment of RV physiology and selected flow/pulmonary haemodynamic monitoring if it will change therapy.

## 1. Standard monitoring and vigilance

Apply full PG18 monitoring appropriate to GA, including continuous ECG/pulse, SpO₂, capnography/ventilation, BP and inspired gas/agent monitoring where relevant, with temperature and neuromuscular monitoring as indicated. ECG should be configured to detect rhythm/ischaemia because arrhythmia and RV perfusion failure are major hazards.

## 2. Arterial catheter

I would place an arterial line before induction if time permits. Systemic hypotension can rapidly reduce RV coronary perfusion and precipitate a spiral of RV failure; beat-to-beat pressure allows immediate vasopressor titration and repeated blood gases for oxygenation, ventilation and acid–base control.

## 3. Echo

Focused TTE or TOE, depending access and expertise, helps assess RV size/function, septal position, LV filling, pericardium and treatment response. It can distinguish low preload from RV pressure overload and guide whether fluid, vasopressor, inotrope or pulmonary vasodilator is appropriate.

## 4. PAC — selected rather than automatic

For severe pulmonary hypertension with unstable or complex physiology, a PAC may be reasonable if serial PA pressure, CO and SvO₂ will guide pulmonary vasodilator, vasopressor/inotrope and fluid decisions. I would balance this against arrhythmia/insertion risks and whether echo plus less invasive monitoring can answer the same questions.

## 5. What I am trying to prevent
- Avoid systemic hypotension, hypoxaemia, hypercapnia and acidosis because each can increase RV strain or reduce RV perfusion.
- Avoid both hypovolaemia and RV overdistension.
- Detect falling CO/RV failure early and treat the cause rather than chasing a CVP target.

items.title: 16. Vascular access in the shocked patient
items.q: Outline your approach to obtaining vascular access in a patient in shock.
items.a:
## Priorities

Rapid, reliable access for **resuscitation, drugs and monitoring**, while treating the cause. Large-bore access takes priority over central lines.

## Approach

1. **Peripheral IV first:** two **large-bore** (14 to 16G) cannulas, antecubital or forearm; use **ultrasound** if veins are not visible. Flow is greatest through short, wide catheters.
2. **Limit attempts:** if access fails after two attempts or about 90 seconds, move to the next option.
3. **Intraosseous (IO) access:** proximal humerus, proximal tibia or distal femur; fast, reliable and suitable for fluids, blood and drugs (flow is slower than a large peripheral line; use pressure). Contraindications: fracture of that bone, infection at the site, previous IO in the same bone, and prosthesis.
4. **Central venous access:** use a large-bore introducer or multi-lumen catheter under ultrasound (internal jugular, subclavian or femoral); femoral is quick and compressible in arrest or major haemorrhage but has a higher infection rate. Avoid delay to resuscitation.
5. **Alternatives:** external jugular vein, venous cutdown (saphenous at the ankle), and in children IO early.
6. **Site considerations:** avoid lower limb access with suspected abdominal or pelvic venous injury; avoid the injured limb.

## Practical points

Use pressure infusers and fluid warmers, secure lines, confirm placement, label arterial or IO lines, give drugs through reliable lines, and replace emergency lines in sterile conditions within 24 to 48 hours.

## Complications

Extravasation, compartment syndrome (IO), infection, pneumothorax, arterial puncture, air embolism and delays to resuscitation.

## Monitoring

Add an arterial line when it will not delay care.

## Self-marking checklist

- Prioritises large-bore peripheral access and ultrasound
- Limits the number of attempts before escalating
- Describes IO access with sites and contraindications
- Describes central and alternative access options with site choice
- Includes practical measures (pressure infusers, warmers)
- Lists complications

items.title: 17. Improving cannulation success and minimising discomfort
items.q: Outline measures to increase the rate of successful intravenous cannulation and to minimise patient discomfort.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Ultrasound-guided peripheral venous cannulation" (BJA Educ): ultrasound improves first-attempt success, guides the choice of catheter gauge and length, and the catheter-to-vein ratio should be 45% or less.

## Improving success

**Planning**
- Identify patients with difficult access (history, obesity, dehydration, chemotherapy, intravenous drug use, oedema, extremes of age).
- Choose the **appropriate site and size**: forearm or antecubital for large cannulas, dorsal hand for small; avoid joints.

**Preparation**
- **Warm** the limb, place it **dependent**, apply a tourniquet and **hydrate** the patient; consider topical nitrate or a heat pack.
- Good lighting, comfortable positioning, and a skilled operator.

**Technique**
- Palpate rather than rely on sight; anchor the vein; correct angle; advance the cannula after flashback.
- **Ultrasound guidance** (dynamic needle-tip positioning), near-infrared vein finders, or an experienced colleague after one or two failed attempts.
- Limit attempts and consider alternatives (IO, central) when urgent.

## Minimising discomfort

- **Explain** and reassure; distraction, music, play specialists for children.
- **Topical local anaesthetic** (EMLA, tetracaine) with time to work, **intradermal lidocaine** (buffered), needle-free jet injection, or vapocoolant spray.
- Small, appropriate cannulas, smooth technique and prompt removal of the tourniquet.
- Anxiolysis or sedation for phobic patients; nitrous oxide for children.
- Pre-warm and avoid repeated attempts.

## Complications to prevent

Haematoma, extravasation, phlebitis, nerve injury and arterial puncture.

## Self-marking checklist

- Lists measures to improve success (site, warming, tourniquet, hydration)
- Describes ultrasound guidance and catheter-to-vein ratio
- Describes limiting attempts and escalation
- Lists topical, intradermal and non-drug comfort measures
- Mentions special groups (children, phobic)
- Names complications

items.title: 18. PICC versus percutaneous CVC for three weeks of therapy
items.q: A patient requires reliable intravenous access for three weeks of antimicrobial therapy. Compare a PICC with a percutaneous central venous catheter and outline how you would minimise the risks of PICC placement and use.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

For three weeks of therapy, I would compare the devices by insertion risk, flow, thrombosis/infection, patient comfort and intended use. A PICC is attractive for prolonged stable therapy but is not automatically safer overall, particularly because thrombosis and occlusion matter. I would then outline risk reduction from device selection through insertion, tip confirmation, maintenance and timely removal.

## 1. Comparison

| Issue | PICC | Percutaneous CVC |
|---|---|---|
| Insertion | Arm insertion avoids insertion-related pneumothorax and major neck/chest arterial injury. | IJ/subclavian/femoral insertion has site-specific mechanical risks. |
| Duration / outpatient care | Well suited to weeks–months and often convenient for mobilisation/outpatient therapy. | Suitable for acute/short-medium term; neck/groin access can be less convenient. |
| Flow | Long/narrow — poor for rapid high-flow resuscitation. | Can provide larger/shorter lumens or introducer access for high-flow therapy. |
| Thrombosis | Upper-extremity thrombosis is an important risk, especially larger/multilumen devices. | Thrombosis risk remains but differs by site/device. |
| Infection | CLABSI risk still requires bundle care. | CLABSI risk also important; site and maintenance matter. |
| Mechanical issues | Malposition, occlusion, migration; no thoracic insertion complication. | Pneumothorax/haemothorax, arterial injury, malposition, bleeding. |

## 2. Minimise PICC risk before insertion
- Confirm that central access is actually required and choose the minimum number of lumens/diameter needed.
- Assess upper-limb veins with ultrasound for patency, size and thrombosis risk; avoid unnecessarily small veins/large catheters.
- Use an appropriate vein/site and full aseptic technique.

## 3. Safe insertion and confirmation

**1. **Use real-time ultrasound-guided venepuncture and a controlled wire/catheter technique.

**2. **Advance to an appropriate central tip position.

**3. **Confirm tip location using the local validated method before using the line for therapies that require central placement.

**4. **Secure and dress the line to reduce migration and contamination.

## 4. Maintenance and removal
- Use an evidence-based central-line infection-prevention bundle and aseptic access technique.
- Monitor for arm swelling/pain, catheter dysfunction, infection and thrombosis.
- Remove the catheter as soon as the indication ends; unnecessary catheter-days create avoidable infection/thrombosis risk.

**Examiner lens:** The historical PICC SAQ expected a balanced comparison rather than “PICC is safer”: lower pneumothorax/major arterial injury risk was offset by thrombosis concerns, and risk reduction needed to include placement confirmation, line-care bundle principles, minimum lumens and removal when no longer required.

items.title: 19. Maximising rapid intravenous fluid/blood delivery and using rapid infusers safely
items.q: Describe the factors that determine the maximum achievable rate of intravenous fluid administration. Outline the issues and hazards associated with rapid infusion devices.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would answer this from fluid mechanics and the complete delivery system: driving pressure, catheter radius/length, fluid viscosity and every resistance in the circuit. I would then discuss rapid-infuser benefits, device/circuit hazards and the physiological consequences of delivering large volumes of cold blood or fluid quickly.

## 1. Determinants of flow

| Factor | Effect on flow / practical meaning |
|---|---|
| Radius / internal diameter | Dominant effect: for laminar flow, flow is proportional to radius⁴. A short large-bore cannula dramatically outperforms a narrow catheter. |
| Length | Flow is inversely proportional to length; long PICCs and standard CVC lumens are poor for rapid resuscitation. |
| Driving pressure | Pressure bags/pumps/rapid infusers increase flow if the circuit can tolerate it. |
| Viscosity | Blood flows more slowly than crystalloid; warming reduces viscosity somewhat and prevents hypothermia. |
| Circuit resistance | Filters, narrow connectors, stopcocks, extension tubing and partially kinked lines reduce flow. |
| Catheter position / vein | Catheter against wall, thrombosis, small vein or extravasation limits effective delivery. |

## 2. Practical setup in major haemorrhage
- Use short large-bore peripheral access or an appropriately large central introducer rather than a long narrow lumen.
- Minimise unnecessary connectors/long extension sets; use compatible blood filters and warming/rapid-infusion circuits.
- Secure lines and check the full circuit before applying high pressure.

## 3. Rapid-infusion device hazards
- Air entrainment/air embolism if the reservoir or tubing is allowed to run dry or air-detection safeguards are bypassed.
- Line/catheter disconnection or rupture with sudden blood/fluid loss into the environment or tissue extravasation.
- Haemolysis risk depends on device, pressure, catheter and product; avoid inappropriate narrow high-resistance circuits.
- Very rapid transfusion increases citrate load/hypocalcaemia, potassium delivery and volume shifts; monitor ionised calcium/electrolytes in major haemorrhage.
- Inadequate warming causes hypothermia and worsens coagulopathy; device warming has temperature/flow limits.
- The rapidity of delivery can outpace clinical reassessment and cause overload if the haemorrhage has been controlled.

## 4. Overall safety principle

A rapid infuser is a delivery tool, not a resuscitation strategy. It should sit within a major-haemorrhage plan with source control, blood-component strategy, warming, calcium/electrolyte monitoring and clear communication about cumulative volume.

items.title: 20. Invasive blood pressure: indications, sites, complications, waveform
items.q: Discuss the indications for and complications of invasive blood pressure monitoring, site selection and the interpretation of the waveform.
items.a:
## Indications

- Anticipated rapid haemodynamic change or major fluid shifts (major, cardiac, vascular, neurosurgery, trauma).
- Severe cardiorespiratory disease, shock or vasoactive infusions.
- Need for **frequent blood sampling** (gases, lactate, glucose).
- NIBP unreliable or impossible (obesity, burns, arrhythmia, positioning).
- Use of cardiac output or dynamic indices (PPV, SVV); controlled hypotension.

## Site selection

| Site | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Radial** | First choice: superficial, collateral flow; Allen test does not reliably predict ischaemia |
| **Brachial** | Larger, but no collateral and risk to median nerve; used if radial unavailable |
| **Femoral** | Large; useful in shock; infection and bleeding risks; higher thrombosis risk in vascular disease |
| **Dorsalis pedis, axillary, ulnar** | Alternatives |

Use **ultrasound** to improve success and reduce attempts.

## Complications

Haematoma, bleeding or disconnection, infection, thrombosis and distal ischaemia, vasospasm, pseudoaneurysm, nerve injury, arterial injection of drugs, and damping or inaccurate readings.

## Interpretation of the waveform

- **Systolic upstroke slope** reflects contractility; the **area under the curve** reflects stroke volume.
- **Dicrotic notch** marks aortic valve closure; a low notch suggests vasodilation, a high notch vasoconstriction.
- **Pulse pressure variation** suggests preload dependency.
- **Systolic overshoot** in an under-damped system overestimates systolic pressure (mean is accurate).
- **Peripheral amplification:** systolic pressure is higher and mean slightly lower at distal sites.
- Arrhythmia, aortic stenosis (slow upstroke) and regurgitation (wide pulse pressure) alter the waveform.
- Confirm accuracy (zero, level, square-wave test), compare with NIBP, and remove when not needed.

## Self-marking checklist

- Gives at least 4 indications
- Compares sites (radial, brachial, femoral)
- Lists complications
- Interprets waveform features (upstroke, notch, pulse pressure variation)
- Discusses damping and peripheral amplification
- Mentions accuracy checks and ultrasound

items.title: 21. Invasive versus non-invasive blood pressure monitoring in morbid obesity
items.q: Evaluate invasive and non-invasive blood pressure monitoring options in a patient with morbid obesity undergoing major surgery.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would evaluate both techniques specifically in obesity, not give generic pros and cons. I would discuss cuff fit/arm geometry and intermittent measurement limitations, then weigh the accuracy and beat-to-beat advantages of an arterial line against technical difficulty and invasive complications.

## 1. Non-invasive BP: advantages in this patient
- Non-invasive and avoids arterial cannulation complications.
- Easy to repeat at different sites/cuff sizes and adequate for many stable patients if a validated, properly fitting cuff is available.
- Useful as an independent comparison even when an arterial line is present.

## 2. Non-invasive BP: obesity-specific limitations
- Large or conical upper arms may make standard cuff fit poor; a cuff that is too small can over-read and an unsuitable cuff can give erratic values.
- Forearm/wrist alternatives may not be interchangeable with upper-arm reference values and should be interpreted cautiously.
- Movement, arrhythmia, severe vasoconstriction and low perfusion worsen oscillometric reliability.
- Intermittent cycling may miss abrupt changes during induction, positioning, pneumoperitoneum or bleeding.

## 3. Invasive arterial BP: advantages
- Beat-to-beat pressure during induction and major surgery; immediate feedback when vasoactive drugs are titrated.
- Frequent arterial sampling for gas, haemoglobin and metabolic assessment.
- Avoids repeated dependence on difficult cuff fit once a reliable arterial system is established.

## 4. Invasive arterial BP: obesity-specific disadvantages and general risks
- Arterial palpation/anatomy and securement may be more difficult; ultrasound can improve success.
- Invasive complications: bleeding/haematoma, infection, thrombosis/ischaemia, pseudoaneurysm, nerve injury and accidental intra-arterial injection.
- The transducer system itself can be wrong: damping, leveling or zeroing errors can produce precise-looking but misleading numbers.

## 5. My choice

For major surgery with anticipated rapid haemodynamic change or vasoactive therapy, I would favour an arterial catheter while retaining an appropriately sized NIBP cuff for cross-checking. For minor stable surgery, a validated correctly sized NIBP setup may be entirely adequate. The decision is driven by procedural/patient risk, not BMI alone.

**Examiner lens:** The 2025.1 report specifically criticised answers that gave generic invasive/NIBP pros and cons without applying them to morbid obesity. The command word was “evaluate”, so both advantages and disadvantages of each method had to be weighed in the obese patient.

items.title: 22. Damped arterial waveform: troubleshooting, damping and leveling
items.q: After radial arterial cannulation, the waveform appears damped and the pressure is 78/52 mmHg while the cuff reads 108/64 mmHg. Describe your assessment of the discrepancy and how you would ensure the arterial line is accurate.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would not immediately treat the arterial-line number. I would first assess the patient and compare independent signals, then troubleshoot the catheter and fluid-filled system, re-level/zero, use a square-wave test to identify damping, and only then decide which pressure is clinically credible.

## 1. Look at the patient and independent measurements
- Check pulse/perfusion, surgical context, ECG and whether there is a genuine low-output state.
- Repeat NIBP with an appropriate cuff and compare another pulse waveform/plethysmograph.
- A small arterial waveform may be genuine in profound low output/vasoconstriction, but a large unexplained discrepancy raises suspicion of measurement error.

## 2. Check the arterial catheter
- Inspect wrist/limb position, catheter kink, partial withdrawal, vasospasm, clot or catheter tip against the vessel wall.
- Check distal perfusion and the insertion site for bleeding/haematoma.

## 3. Check the tubing/transducer system
- Air bubbles, clot, long/compliant tubing, multiple stopcocks and loose connections commonly overdamp the trace.
- Make sure the flush bag is pressurised and the line is patent; remove bubbles/clot and unnecessary compliance/resistance.
- Re-level the transducer to the intended anatomical reference and re-zero to atmosphere if required.

## 4. Damping and the square-wave test

| Pattern | Effect | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Overdamped | Slurred upstroke, low systolic/high diastolic, narrow pulse pressure; MAP often less affected. | Air/clot/compliant tubing/kink/partial occlusion. |
| Underdamped / resonant | Systolic overshoot, low diastolic, ringing; MAP often less affected. | Stiff/high-frequency system, catheter whip/resonance. |

Briefly activate the fast flush to generate a square wave. Excess oscillations after release suggest underdamping; a sluggish return with minimal oscillation suggests overdamping. The test assesses the monitoring system, not the patient.

## 5. Leveling in unusual positions

Hydrostatic pressure changes by about 0.74 mmHg per centimetre vertical height. A transducer below the reference level reads falsely high and above it falsely low. In beach-chair/sitting surgery, if cerebral perfusion is the target, I must account for the vertical distance between the heart and brain rather than assuming a heart-level MAP represents cerebral arterial pressure.

## 6. Final action

Until the system is corrected, I would use the pressure that best fits the patient and independent measurements, with particular attention to MAP. I would not titrate potent vasopressors to an obviously unreliable trace.

items.title: 23. Goal-directed haemodynamic therapy in major abdominal surgery
items.q: Discuss the principles, evidence and practical conduct of goal-directed haemodynamic therapy for a high-risk patient undergoing major abdominal surgery.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "The place of goal-directed haemodynamic therapy" (BJA Educ): GDT is a bundle of fluid, vasoactive drugs and oxygen guided by monitored flow to improve outcome; it reduces hospital stay and complications (acute kidney injury, respiratory failure, wound infection); its effect on mortality is uncertain.

## Principles

GDT augments **blood flow and oxygen delivery** using combinations of **fluids, inotropes, vasopressors and oxygen**, guided by a cardiac output monitor. It targets measured flow variables (stroke volume, cardiac output, SVV, oxygen delivery) rather than arbitrary pressure or volume.

## Who benefits

The **high-risk surgical patient**: predicted mortality above 5% (above 20% for extremely high-risk), poor functional capacity (below 4 METs, or anaerobic threshold below 11 mL/kg/min on CPET), major vascular, upper or lower GI and hepatobiliary surgery. This group is about 12.5% of surgical activity but accounts for about 80% of deaths.

## Practical conduct

1. Identify high-risk patients preoperatively and plan critical care.
2. Insert an arterial line and a minimally invasive CO monitor; confirm validity conditions.
3. Begin with a **fluid challenge** (for example 250 mL); repeat while stroke volume rises by 10% or more.
4. When stroke volume plateaus, stop fluid; if the target is not achieved, add **inotrope** (low-dose dobutamine) or vasopressor (noradrenaline) to maintain MAP.
5. Maintain haemoglobin, oxygenation and temperature; extend the protocol into the early postoperative period.
6. Use lactate, urine output and clinical perfusion as cross-checks.

## Evidence

Early studies and meta-analyses show fewer complications and shorter stay; large pragmatic trials (OPTIMISE and OPTIMISE II) did not show a clear benefit on their primary endpoints, so the benefit is greatest in the highest-risk patients and with consistent protocol use. Mortality benefit is not proven.

## Alternatives and cautions

Restrictive or ERAS fluid regimens and avoidance of hypotension are also valid; benefits depend on the baseline fluid practice, monitor reliability and timeliness of action.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines GDT (flow-guided bundle of fluids, vasoactives, oxygen)
- Identifies the high-risk patient with numbers
- Describes the protocol steps including a fluid challenge and inotrope use
- Notes the benefits on complications and stay
- States that mortality benefit is uncertain
- Notes contrary or neutral trials and restrictive alternatives

items.title: 24. Indicators of tissue oxygenation in resuscitation
items.q: Outline the clinical use and limitations of indicators of tissue oxygenation (base deficit, lactate, mixed venous saturation and others) in resuscitation.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Does near-infrared spectroscopy play a role in ICU?" (BJA Educ): NIRS can help identify low cardiac output alongside serial lactate and mixed venous samples, and has a growing role in sepsis and poor perfusion.

## Why measure

Oxygen delivery (cardiac output x arterial oxygen content) and consumption must balance. Pressure and heart rate are crude surrogates; measures of tissue oxygenation show **whether perfusion is adequate**.

## Indicators

| Indicator | Use | Limitations |
|---|---|---|
| **Lactate** | Raised (above 2 mmol/L) suggests anaerobic metabolism; **clearance** over 2 to 6 hours predicts outcome | Also raised by adrenaline, liver failure, metformin, thiamine deficiency, regional beds; slow to change |
| **Base deficit** | Metabolic acidosis from tissue hypoperfusion; grades haemorrhage severity | Affected by chloride, renal disease, alcohol |
| **Mixed venous saturation (SvO2) or central venous (ScvO2)** | Balance of delivery and consumption; normal 65 to 75% | High in sepsis or shunt; needs a PAC or CVC; no outcome benefit shown in trials |
| **Venous-arterial CO2 gap** | Above about 6 mmHg suggests inadequate flow | Needs a central line; interpretation depends on ScvO2 |
| **Capillary refill time** | Bedside, peripheral perfusion | Subjective; but CRT-targeted resuscitation was non-inferior to lactate in trials |
| **Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS)** | Non-invasive regional (cerebral or muscle) oxygenation trend | Reference values vary; extracranial contamination; limited outcome evidence |
| **Urine output, gastric tonometry, sublingual microcirculation** | Organ and microvascular perfusion | Research or limited use |

## Application

Use **several indicators together** with clinical perfusion and flow monitoring; target normalisation of lactate and perfusion rather than a single number, and **watch the trend**.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains the delivery-consumption balance
- Lists at least four indicators with uses
- Gives limitations for each (lactate causes, SvO2 in sepsis)
- Mentions NIRS and the CO2 gap or capillary refill
- Recommends combining indicators and trends
- Notes the lack of outcome benefit for single-target protocols

items.title: 25. Fluids and goal-directed therapy in septic shock
items.q: Discuss the role of intravenous fluid and goal-directed therapy in the resuscitation of septic shock.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Fluids in sepsis" (BJA Educ 2026): evidence shows harm associated with intravenous fluid therapy in sepsis; the revised Starling principle highlights the endothelial glycocalyx; restrictive strategies appear safe in selected patients; fluid deresuscitation may reduce harm from overload.

## Pathophysiology

Sepsis causes vasodilation, capillary leak and relative hypovolaemia. The **revised Starling principle** places the **endothelial glycocalyx** and the subglycocalyx space at the centre: damage allows leak, and much of a crystalloid bolus does not remain intravascular.

## Fluid therapy

- Early fluid for hypoperfusion is standard (international guidance suggests 30 mL/kg within 3 hours on low-quality evidence), but a positive fluid balance and a high CVP are associated with higher mortality.
- Use **balanced crystalloids**. Consider albumin if large volumes are needed.
- Give fluid as **boluses with reassessment** and a measure of fluid responsiveness (passive leg raise, dynamic indices, echo, capillary refill), because only about half of patients are responders.
- **Restrictive strategies** (early vasopressors and limited fluid) appear safe in selected patients; **deresuscitation** (diuretics or ultrafiltration) is used for overload once the patient is stable.

## Vasopressors

**Noradrenaline** is first line; add vasopressin and consider hydrocortisone and an inotrope for myocardial dysfunction. Early vasopressors via a peripheral line are acceptable.

## Goal-directed targets

MAP 65 mmHg, lactate clearance, capillary refill time, urine output, ScvO2 (early goal-directed therapy using ScvO2 was not superior to usual care in ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe), cardiac output and echo.

## Principle

Treat sepsis as a combination of **source control, antimicrobials, appropriate fluid and vasopressors**, individualised by repeated assessment.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains the pathophysiology including the glycocalyx
- Gives the role and limits of initial fluid
- Describes dynamic assessment of fluid responsiveness
- Mentions restrictive strategies and deresuscitation
- States noradrenaline first line and adjuncts
- Notes that ScvO2-targeted therapy was no better than usual care

items.title: 26. PAC insertion technique and pressure waveforms
items.q: Describe the technique of insertion of a pulmonary artery catheter and the pressure waveforms you would see.
items.a:
## Preparation

Indication and consent, sterile technique with full barrier precautions, **ECG, defibrillator**, resuscitation drugs and an experienced operator. Check the catheter balloon (1.5 mL air) and flush the lumens. Use a sheath introducer in the right internal jugular vein (shortest path) under ultrasound; Trendelenburg position.

## Insertion

1. Pass the catheter through the introducer with the balloon deflated to about 20 cm.
2. **Inflate the balloon** and advance with flow, watching the pressure trace.
3. Approximate depths from the right IJ: **RA 15 to 20 cm, RV 25 to 35 cm, PA 40 to 50 cm, wedge 45 to 55 cm**.
4. **Deflate the balloon** after wedging, confirm a PA trace and withdraw if the catheter wedges with the balloon deflated.
5. Secure, dress and obtain a chest X-ray (tip in zone 3, no loop or kink).

## Waveforms

| Chamber | Pressure and features |
|---|---|
| **RA** | Mean 2 to 8 mmHg: a, c, v waves; x and y descents |
| **RV** | 15 to 30 / 0 to 8 mmHg: rapid systolic upstroke; **diastolic pressure falls to near zero** |
| **PA** | 15 to 30 / 4 to 12 mmHg: dicrotic notch; **diastolic step-up** |
| **Wedge (PAOP)** | 6 to 12 mmHg: a and v waves, lower amplitude; reflects left atrial pressure |

## Complications and cautions

Arrhythmias (RBBB, and complete heart block in pre-existing LBBB), PA rupture (avoid overinflation and leaving the balloon wedged), pulmonary infarction, knotting, valve damage, infection and thrombosis. Cautious with left bundle branch block, severe pulmonary hypertension and anticoagulation.

## Reading the wedge

Measure at end-expiration, with the transducer levelled to the left atrium, in zone 3 where the tip lies below the left atrium. Large v waves indicate mitral regurgitation.

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes preparation and monitoring needs
- States insertion depths or landmarks for each chamber
- Describes the RA, RV, PA and wedge waveforms
- Mentions balloon inflation and deflation
- Lists complications including PA rupture and arrhythmia
- Gives wedge measurement technique

items.title: 27. Central venous routes, ultrasound and arterial cannulation
items.q: Compare the internal jugular, subclavian and femoral routes for central venous access, discuss the role of ultrasound, and outline how you would prevent and manage inadvertent arterial cannulation.
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2019, "Preventing vascular damage during central venous catheter insertion via the internal jugular vein" (Bath, Deacon, Jones).

## Route comparison

| Route | Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|---|
| **Internal jugular** | Compressible, easy to see on ultrasound, low pneumothorax risk (below 0.2%) | Arterial puncture 6 to 9%; neck mobility and patient comfort |
| **Subclavian** | Lower infection and thrombosis risk, comfortable | Pneumothorax 1.5 to 3%, haemothorax, non-compressible bleeding |
| **Femoral** | Quick, away from the airway, compressible | Highest total complications (13 to 19%), arterial puncture 9 to 15%, higher infection and thrombosis rates |

Choose the site on clinical need and operator skill; IJ or subclavian are preferred unless contraindicated.

## Preventing vascular injury

- Operator **experience and supervision**; **three or more attempts** raises complications about six-fold, so call for help.
- **Trendelenburg** position with head rotation **below 45 degrees**.
- **Real-time ultrasound**, following the needle tip in short axis; confirm the guidewire in the vein by ultrasound.
- Pressure monitoring (column manometry) or blood gas to confirm venous placement **before dilating**.
- Advance the wire gently; check the dilator moves freely over it; aspirate and flush all lumens.
- Confirm tip position at the **atrial-caval junction** (chest X-ray, fluoroscopy or ECG-guidance).

## Inadvertent arterial cannulation

Suspect with bright blood or pulsatile flow, high-pressure alarms or an arterial trace. **Small needle** puncture: remove and apply pressure for 5 to 10 minutes. **Large-bore catheter in a carotid or subclavian artery: do not simply pull** (haemorrhage, stroke, pseudoaneurysm): obtain imaging and **vascular or endovascular** surgical advice and plan the removal. Femoral artery: pull and pressure or closure device.

## Self-marking checklist

- Compares the three routes with complication rates
- States the benefits of ultrasound and real-time technique
- Lists prevention (positioning, attempts, confirm venous placement before dilation)
- Names atrial-caval junction tip position
- Distinguishes managing needle puncture from large-bore arterial cannulation
- Advises vascular team involvement

items.title: 28. Perioperative fluid requirements and choice of fluid in major abdominal surgery
items.q: Discuss the factors determining perioperative fluid requirements and the choice of fluid in an adult having major abdominal surgery.
items.a:
## Requirements

- **Maintenance:** about 1 to 1.5 mL/kg/h for the fasting patient (water, sodium and potassium), balanced against reduced urine output after surgery.
- **Fasting deficit:** routine large preoperative deficit replacement is no longer recommended; allow clear fluid until 2 hours before surgery, and correct measured deficits.
- **Losses:** blood loss, evaporative and tissue losses (insensible, exposure), ascites, bowel preparation and nasogastric output.
- **Vasodilation** from anaesthesia and neuraxial block (use vasopressors rather than large volumes).
- Patient factors: age, cardiac, renal and hepatic disease, sepsis, pre-existing dehydration.

## Strategy

- **Restrictive versus liberal:** very restrictive regimens risk hypoperfusion and AKI; very liberal regimens cause oedema, ileus and poor wound healing. The **RELIEF** trial found a restrictive regimen did not improve disability-free survival and increased acute kidney injury. Aim for **zero balance (euvolaemia)**.
- **Goal-directed therapy** in high-risk surgery (see monitoring).
- Enhanced recovery pathways: early oral intake, minimal IV fluid, vasopressors for hypotension.

## Choice of fluid

| Fluid | Comments |
|---|---|
| **Balanced crystalloid** (Plasma-Lyte, Hartmann) | Preferred; less hyperchloraemic acidosis than saline (SMART, PLUS) |
| **0.9% saline** | Hyperchloraemic acidosis and AKI risk in large volumes; suited to hyponatraemia or hypochloraemia |
| **Albumin** | Specific roles (cirrhosis, large paracentesis, sepsis in selected patients); costly |
| **Synthetic colloids (starches)** | Increased AKI and mortality: avoid |
| **Blood** | Replace for haemorrhage by triggers (haemoglobin 70 to 80 g/L or physiology) |
| **Glucose** | Only to prevent hypoglycaemia in selected patients; hypotonic fluids risk hyponatraemia |

## Monitoring response

Blood pressure, heart rate, urine output, lactate, and where indicated a flow monitor; reassess after each bolus.

## Self-marking checklist

- Gives maintenance rates and no routine deficit replacement
- Lists ongoing losses and the effect of anaesthesia
- Discusses restrictive versus liberal regimens and the RELIEF trial
- Prefers balanced crystalloids and explains saline risks
- States the role of albumin and avoidance of starches
- Mentions monitoring and goal-directed therapy

items.title: 29. Perioperative fluid prescription for a low-risk adult
items.q: A healthy 70 kg adult is fasting for an uncomplicated two-hour elective operation with minimal expected blood loss and early postoperative oral intake. Describe and justify your perioperative intravenous fluid plan.
items.a:
## A high-scoring structure

I would first decide whether IV fluid is required at all, then separate maintenance from resuscitation and replacement. In this low-risk patient I would avoid routine replacement of a large “fasting deficit” or theoretical third-space loss, use a balanced isotonic crystalloid only for actual need, and aim for early return to oral intake.

## 1. Preoperative considerations

With modern fasting practice, many patients can have clear fluids until relatively close to surgery according to local policy, so the historical calculation of a large fasting deficit is usually inappropriate. I would assess actual intake, vomiting/diarrhoea, diuretics, renal/cardiac disease and clinical signs of dehydration rather than assume hypovolaemia from fasting alone.

## 2. Intraoperative plan
- If IV fluid is needed, a balanced isotonic crystalloid is a reasonable default.
- For a short low-risk case with minimal losses, use a modest rate sufficient for actual maintenance/therapy rather than a fixed large-volume formula.
- Replace measured blood or other losses according to their nature. Significant blood loss becomes a blood-management problem, not simply more crystalloid.
- If hypotension occurs, identify vasodilation, low preload, pump failure, arrhythmia or obstruction before giving repeated fluid.

## 3. Maintenance framework if oral intake is delayed

A common adult starting point is roughly 25–30 mL/kg/day of water with approximately 1 mmol/kg/day each of sodium, potassium and chloride and limited glucose to reduce starvation ketosis, adjusted for age, renal/cardiac function, other intake and laboratory values. For this 70 kg adult that is a daily framework, not a reason to infuse the entire requirement during the two-hour operation.

## 4. Postoperative plan

Encourage oral intake when safe and stop IV maintenance once it is no longer needed. Reassess fluid balance, urine output, electrolytes and symptoms rather than continuing fluid by inertia.

items.title: 2026.1 Q2: Assessing intravascular volume and the limits of CVP
items.q: List the methods available to assess the intravascular volume status of a patient. (30%) Discuss the limitations of using central venous pressure for assessing intravascular volume status. (70%)
items.model:
## Methods of assessment

| Category | Methods |
|---|---|
| Clinical | History (losses, intake), heart rate, blood pressure, postural change, capillary refill, skin turgor, mucous membranes, JVP, urine output, weight and fluid balance |
| Laboratory | Lactate and base deficit, urea:creatinine ratio, urinary sodium, haematocrit |
| Invasive static | Central venous pressure (CVP), pulmonary artery occlusion pressure |
| Invasive dynamic | Pulse pressure variation (PPV), stroke volume variation (SVV), response to a fluid challenge, cardiac output monitoring (pulse contour, oesophageal Doppler) |
| Non-invasive | Passive leg raise, echocardiography (IVC collapsibility, LV size, VTI variation), lung ultrasound, plethysmographic variability |

## Limitations of CVP

CVP is a **pressure**, not a volume. It reflects right atrial filling pressure and correlates poorly with blood volume and with fluid responsiveness.

**Measurement errors**
- Transducer not levelled to the right atrium (mid-axillary line) or not zeroed.
- Damped or over-damped trace, air bubbles, catheter tip malposition or kinking.
- Reading taken during the respiratory cycle rather than at **end-expiration**.

**Non-volume factors that alter CVP**
- **Intrathoracic pressure:** positive pressure ventilation and PEEP raise CVP; so does tension pneumothorax or tamponade.
- **Patient position** (head-down, prone, lateral) and **intra-abdominal pressure** (pneumoperitoneum, ascites).
- **Venous tone and compliance:** anaesthesia, vasopressors and sympathetic tone alter the pressure for the same volume.
- **Cardiac factors:** tricuspid regurgitation, RV failure, pulmonary hypertension, poor LV compliance and arrhythmias raise CVP regardless of volume.

**Interpretation limits**
- A **single value** is less useful than a **trend** or the response to a fluid challenge.
- A low CVP does not predict a response to fluid, and a high CVP does not exclude hypovolaemia.
- No threshold value is reliable; the same number means different things in different patients.

## Practical use

Use CVP as one item among several: trend it, combine it with dynamic indices, echo and perfusion markers (lactate, urine output, capillary refill), and judge volume by the **response to treatment**.

items.title: 2025.2 Q8: TTE in the unstable anaesthetised patient
items.q: Evaluate the use of transthoracic echocardiography in assessing the haemodynamically unstable patient under general anaesthesia.
items.model:
## Why TTE intraoperatively

Hypotension under anaesthesia has many causes (hypovolaemia, vasodilation, myocardial depression or ischaemia, embolism, tamponade, tension pneumothorax) and the anaesthetist needs a rapid answer. A **goal-directed TTE** is a short, bedside, repeatable examination by a trained operator designed to exclude major abnormalities and guide therapy.

## Advantages

- **Differentiates shock states** in minutes: hypovolaemia (small, hyperdynamic, "kissing" LV; collapsing IVC), distributive (hyperdynamic LV, normal or large IVC), cardiogenic (poor LV or RV function, dilated chambers), obstructive (pericardial effusion, dilated RV with septal shift in pulmonary embolus).
- **Guides treatment and its response:** fluid challenge (LV size, IVC, VTI change), inotropes, vasopressors, and detects the response in real time.
- Non-invasive, no insertion risk, no need to interrupt the operation if access is possible; repeated assessment; extends to lung ultrasound (B-lines, pneumothorax, effusion).
- Available without setting up a TOE probe or specific equipment; quick compared with a PA catheter.

## Limitations in this setting

- **Access:** drapes, surgical field, position (prone, lateral, head-down), dressings or obesity make the parasternal and apical windows hard; the subcostal window is often the only one and may be obstructed by laparotomy or lung disease.
- **Image quality:** ventilated lungs, hyperinflation, emphysema and PEEP reduce windows; poor in 10 to 30% of patients.
- **Operator dependence:** training and experience required (ANZCA PS46 sets supervised study numbers); risk of misinterpretation and incorrect diagnosis.
- **Interpretation confounders:** positive pressure ventilation, arrhythmia, vasopressors, valvular disease and pre-existing abnormalities limit measures such as IVC size and variation.
- **Intermittent**, not continuous; requires hands, time and an assistant, and cannot replace continuous monitoring; **TOE** is better for continuous monitoring and when TTE windows fail.
- Not a substitute for clinical judgement; findings must be integrated with the whole picture.

## Overall

TTE is a valuable first-line adjunct that changes management in many unstable patients, provided the operator is trained and the question is focused. Use TOE if TTE fails or surgery blocks access.

items.title: 2025.1 Q1: Invasive and non-invasive BP monitoring in morbid obesity
items.q: Evaluate the use of invasive and of non-invasive blood pressure monitoring options in a patient with morbid obesity.
items.model:
## Why obesity changes the question

Obesity brings conical, large arms, difficult cannulation, frequent comorbidity (OSA, hypertension, obesity hypoventilation, cardiac disease), pneumoperitoneum and head-up positioning in bariatric surgery. Each monitoring option should be weighed against these.

## Non-invasive (oscillometric cuff)

**Advantages**
- No insertion risk, quick to apply, cheap and adequate for many bariatric cases.
- A correctly sized cuff on the upper arm gives acceptable accuracy.

**Disadvantages in obesity**
- **Cuff size error:** a cuff too small **overestimates** pressure (bladder width should be about 40% and length 80% of arm circumference); too large underestimates.
- **Conical arm** causes cuff slip and poor fit; tapered cuffs help.
- Forearm, calf or wrist cuffs are less accurate and unreliable at extremes of pressure.
- Intermittent only (every 1 to 3 minutes), so rapid changes (induction, pneumoperitoneum) are missed; frequent cycling risks nerve and skin injury.
- Oscillometry degrades with arrhythmia, shivering, movement and low-flow states.

## Invasive (arterial line)

**Advantages**
- **Accurate regardless of arm size**, beat-to-beat, and detects abrupt changes.
- Allows **arterial blood gases** (OSA, hypoventilation, pneumoperitoneum, high PEEP, recruitment manoeuvres) and pulse pressure or stroke volume variation.
- Useful where the cuff cannot be placed because of limb shape or positioning.

**Disadvantages**
- Difficult cannulation (landmarks hidden, oedema); use ultrasound. Radial is preferred; femoral raises infection risk.
- Haematoma, infection, thrombosis, ischaemia, nerve injury, and risk of disconnection and bleeding.
- Zeroing and levelling errors, damping, cost and time.

## Judgement

Use a non-invasive cuff with the **correct size** for low-risk, short cases. Choose an arterial line for high-risk patients (OSA with cardiopulmonary disease, BMI very high with poor cuff fit, major surgery, expected need for gases, haemodynamic instability). Document the reason and confirm agreement with the cuff.

items.title: 2023.2 Q4: Evaluating the pulmonary artery catheter
items.q: Evaluate the usage of the pulmonary artery catheter in anaesthesia.
items.model:
## What it provides

A flow-directed, balloon-tipped (Swan-Ganz) catheter measures:

- **Pulmonary artery pressures** (systolic, diastolic, mean), right atrial pressure and the pulmonary artery occlusion pressure (surrogate for left atrial pressure).
- **Cardiac output** (thermodilution; continuous with a heated filament) and **mixed venous oxygen saturation** (SvO2).
- **Derived values:** PVR and SVR, stroke volume, oxygen delivery and consumption.

## Utility in practice

- **Right heart and pulmonary circulation:** diagnosis and grading of pulmonary hypertension (right heart catheterisation is required), RV failure, and guiding pulmonary vasodilators.
- **Distinguishing left from right ventricular failure** and shock states (cardiogenic, septic, mixed), titrating vasopressors, inotropes and fluids in complex cases.
- Cardiac surgery (high-risk, LV or RV failure, transplantation), liver transplantation, major vascular surgery with pulmonary hypertension and selected intensive care patients (cardiogenic shock, sepsis, ARDS).
- **Continuous** monitoring of trends and the response to therapy.

## Evidence

Randomised trials in intensive care and high-risk surgery (for example ESCAPE, PAC-Man, FACTT) showed **no survival benefit** and raised safety concerns; less invasive cardiac output monitors, echocardiography and pulse contour devices have replaced it for many uses. Advocates argue it remains valuable "in the right patient, right setting and right heart", with protocolised use and trained operators.

## Risks

- Insertion: central venous access complications, **arrhythmias** (ventricular ectopy, VT, RBBB, and complete heart block if pre-existing LBBB), knotting.
- Use: **pulmonary artery rupture** (high mortality; age, anticoagulation, pulmonary hypertension, balloon over-inflation or distal migration), pulmonary infarction, valve damage, endocarditis, thrombosis, infection.
- Misinterpretation: wedge pressure affected by PEEP, mitral disease, ventilation and positioning; waveform errors and damping.

## Contraindications

Tricuspid or pulmonary mechanical valve, right heart mass or thrombus, severe coagulopathy, and caution with LBBB, pacemaker leads and severe pulmonary hypertension.

## Overall

Selective, expert use only; compare with echocardiography and pulse contour devices, and use alongside clinical judgement.

items.title: 2017.1 Q7: Maximum IV flow rates and rapid infusion devices
items.source: Past SAQ 2017.1 Q7 · pass rate not reported
items.q: Describe the factors that determine the maximum achievable rate of intravenous fluid administration. (50%) Outline the issues associated with the use of rapid infusion devices. (50%)
items.model:
## Determinants of flow

Flow through a rigid tube follows the **Hagen-Poiseuille** relation:

**Q = (pressure gradient x pi x r^4) / (8 x viscosity x length)**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Radius** | Flow rises with the fourth power of radius: a 14G cannula runs at about 250 mL/min against about 35 mL/min for 22G |
| **Length** | Short cannulas and large introducer sheaths beat long central lines; extension tubing and three-way taps add resistance |
| **Pressure gradient** | Height of the bag (1 m is about 75 mmHg), a pressure bag (300 mmHg) or a pump |
| **Viscosity** | Blood is about three times as viscous as crystalloid; warming reduces viscosity; dilution with saline helps |
| **Other** | Kinks, filters, smaller drip chambers, small or spastic vein, venous pressure, extravasation, cannula position |

Flow is also turbulent at high rates, so the relation is approximate.

## Rapid infusion devices

Rapid infusion systems (for example Belmont, Level 1) combine a reservoir, pump, warmer and air detector, and can deliver **hundreds of mL/min to over 1 L/min**.

**Issues**
- **Air embolism**: the major complication. Needs a bubble trap and air detector, primed lines and vigilant staff.
- **Hypothermia or overheating**: warmer failure, or excessive heating causing haemolysis.
- **Citrate toxicity** (hypocalcaemia), **hyperkalaemia**, acidosis and dilutional coagulopathy with large transfusion.
- **Fluid overload**, pulmonary oedema, abdominal compartment syndrome and rebound hypotension when stopped.
- **Access complications**: extravasation, vein rupture, thrombophlebitis and infection; needs large-bore access.
- **Haemolysis** from high pressures or small cannulas.
- **Practical**: equipment failure, staff training, set-up time, cost, availability and aseptic handling.

## Management

Choose the shortest, widest access, warm all fluids, prime and check lines for air, monitor temperature, calcium, potassium and coagulation, and have a trained operator.

items.title: 2015.2 Q9: PICC versus percutaneous CVC for three weeks
items.q: A patient requires vascular access for three weeks. a. List the advantages and disadvantages of a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC line) compared to a percutaneous central venous catheter (CVL). (50%) b. Outline the methods by which you would minimize the risks associated with the placement of a PICC line. (50%)
items.model:
## a. PICC versus CVL for three weeks

**Advantages of a PICC**
- **Safer to insert:** no pneumothorax, haemothorax or carotid or subclavian arterial injury; can be placed in coagulopathic patients and by nurse or radiology teams.
- Suitable for weeks to months; comfortable and can be used at home.
- Lower insertion cost and avoids the neck and chest (better for patient mobility, tracheostomy, neck surgery).
- Less risk of the early complications of a CVL.

**Disadvantages of a PICC**
- **More upper limb venous thrombosis** (higher than CVL), phlebitis and occlusion in the long term.
- **Smaller lumen**, lower flow: poor for resuscitation, large-volume or rapid infusion.
- Tip malposition or migration; need to confirm position.
- Uses the veins of the arm: avoid in renal failure or planned fistula.
- Bloodstream infection risk is not clearly lower than a CVL in hospital patients.
- Less accurate CVP measurements; limits arm movement; dressing and care needs.

## b. Minimising the risks of PICC insertion

**Appropriate use**
- Confirm a clear indication and expected duration; choose the **fewest lumens** and the smallest suitable catheter; review daily and remove early.

**Insertion**
- Trained operator. **Ultrasound-guided** puncture of the basilic or brachial vein, with a catheter-to-vein ratio of 45% or less to reduce thrombosis.
- **CLAB bundle:** hand hygiene, maximal barrier precautions, chlorhexidine skin preparation, sterile dressing, avoiding the groin.
- Avoid the arm with a fistula, lymphoedema or recent surgery.

**Confirm placement**
- Tip at the cavo-atrial junction, confirmed by ECG-guidance, fluoroscopy or chest X-ray; check for arterial puncture and flush all lumens.

**Aftercare**
- Securement device, regular dressing change, flush protocol, monitor for thrombosis and infection, document and remove when no longer needed.

items.title: 2013.2 Q3: Stroke volume variation and haemodynamic optimisation
items.q: a. Outline the principles of stroke volume variation (SVV) measurement. (50%) b. Describe how SVV measurement can be used to assist haemodynamic optimisation in a patient undergoing major elective abdominal surgery. (50%)
items.model:
## a. Principles

SVV is the **percentage variation in stroke volume over the respiratory cycle** during positive pressure ventilation:

**SVV = (SVmax - SVmin) / SVmean x 100**

- **Heart-lung interaction:** inspiration raises intrathoracic pressure, reducing venous return and RV preload and (after a lag of a few beats) LV preload; on the steep part of the Frank-Starling curve this lowers stroke volume at expiration. A large variation means the ventricle is **preload dependent and fluid responsive**; a small variation means the heart is on the flat part of the curve.
- Measured from the arterial waveform by **pulse contour analysis** (for example FloTrac, PiCCO, LiDCO) or from stroke volume by Doppler. Pulse pressure variation (PPV) is the same principle using pulse pressure.
- Typical threshold: **above about 10 to 13%** predicts a rise in stroke volume with a fluid bolus.

**Validity conditions:** controlled ventilation with tidal volume of 8 mL/kg or more, sinus rhythm, closed chest, no spontaneous breathing, normal abdominal pressure, normal RV and no high-PEEP. In other settings it is unreliable (arrhythmia, spontaneous breathing, low tidal volume, open abdomen or chest, RV failure, raised intra-abdominal pressure).

## b. Use for optimisation in major abdominal surgery

1. Insert an arterial line connected to a pulse contour monitor (or use another cardiac output monitor), and confirm the validity conditions.
2. Set a **goal-directed protocol**: baseline SVV; if it exceeds the threshold, give a **fluid bolus** (for example 250 mL crystalloid or colloid) and watch the response in SV or cardiac output.
3. **Repeat boluses while stroke volume rises** (10% or more) and SVV falls; stop when SV plateaus.
4. If blood pressure or cardiac output stays low despite a **low SVV**, use **inotropes or vasopressors** rather than more fluid, avoiding both hypovolaemia and fluid overload.
5. Aim to avoid tissue hypoperfusion; use with lactate, urine output and clinical assessment; apply through the intra- and early postoperative period.
6. Recognise limits and cross-check with other monitors.

Goal-directed therapy in high-risk surgery reduces complications and hospital stay, although its effect on mortality is uncertain.

items.title: 2013.1 Q3: Damped radial arterial trace
items.q: An elderly patient is to undergo operative fixation of a fractured neck of femur. A radial arterial line is inserted prior to induction, and when transduced, the trace appears damped. a. What are the possible causes for the trace to appear damped in this patient? (50%) b. Outline the steps you would take to ensure the accuracy of your arterial line. (50%)
items.model:
## a. Causes of a damped trace

**1. True damping of the system** (the commonest cause, correctable)
- Air bubbles or **clot or fibrin** in the catheter or tubing.
- **Kinked** cannula or tubing, cannula against the vessel wall or in spasm, or positional (wrist flexed).
- Tubing too long or too compliant; loose connection; extra taps.
- Flush bag **pressure below 300 mmHg** or empty; transducer fault; closed stopcock.

**2. Inaccurate reading**
- Transducer not zeroed or levelled; wrong scale or setting; monitor error.

**3. A true reading in a patient with a clinical reason**
- **Hypovolaemia or shock** (blood loss, dehydration) with low stroke volume.
- **Peripheral vascular disease** or atheroma in the radial or subclavian artery, and vasoconstriction.
- **Aortic stenosis** (slow upstroke), arrhythmia (AF), low cardiac output or tamponade.
- Cold peripheries and hypothermia.

## b. Ensuring accuracy

1. **Exclude damping:** check the system from patient to transducer, look for kinks and bubbles, flush, aspirate, check the pressure bag, and perform a **fast-flush (square wave) test** (a good system shows one or two oscillations before settling; many oscillations mean under-damping, a slurred return means over-damping).
2. **Check calibration:** zero to atmosphere, level to the right atrium (mid-axillary line, 4th intercostal space), correct scale.
3. **Compare with the NIBP** on the opposite arm: the mean should agree within about 5 to 10 mmHg; discrepancy needs investigation.
4. **Assess the patient:** palpate the pulse, capillary refill, pulse oximeter waveform, ECG, and look at the clinical picture.
5. If doubt remains, reposition the cannula or limb, or **re-site** (brachial, femoral, dorsalis pedis), using ultrasound.
6. Repeat zeroing and the square-wave test periodically and with position changes.

items.title: 2007.1 Q5: Continuous mixed venous oxygen saturation in ICU
items.source: Past SAQ 2007.1 Q5 · pass rate not reported
items.q: Discuss the usefulness of the continuous measurement of mixed venous oxygen saturation in the intensive care patient.
items.model:
## What it measures

Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) reflects the balance between oxygen delivery and consumption:

**SvO2 = SaO2 - VO2 / (cardiac output x Hb x 1.34)**

Normal is about **65 to 75%**. It is measured continuously by **fibre-optic reflectance oximetry** in a pulmonary artery catheter; central venous (ScvO2) is a less invasive alternative that runs a few per cent higher.

## Usefulness

- **Early warning:** a fall indicates delivery has dropped or consumption has risen (low cardiac output, anaemia, hypoxaemia, fever, shivering, agitation, sepsis), often before hypotension.
- **Continuous trend:** reveals the effect of interventions immediately (suctioning, turning, weaning, inotrope or transfusion changes) and avoids repeated blood sampling.
- **Guiding therapy:** helps titrate cardiac output, haemoglobin and oxygen delivery, and judge readiness for weaning.
- **Triage of cause:** the low value prompts the question of which of cardiac output, haemoglobin, SaO2 or VO2 has changed.

## Limitations

- A **normal or high** SvO2 does not exclude tissue hypoxia: in sepsis or with cyanide toxicity, shunting and impaired extraction raise SvO2; hypothermia and anaesthesia reduce VO2; a wedged catheter or left-to-right shunt gives falsely high values.
- Needs a PAC (arrhythmia, pulmonary artery injury, infection, cost); drift, calibration and artefact (catheter against the vessel wall, low flow).
- It is a **global** measure and cannot detect regional ischaemia.
- **No proven outcome benefit:** trials of supranormal oxygen delivery targets (SvO2-guided therapy) and PAC use showed no mortality benefit, and ScvO2-guided sepsis protocols were no better than usual care.

## Overall

Continuous SvO2 is a useful **trend monitor** in selected high-risk patients with a PAC in place, interpreted with lactate, clinical perfusion and echo, but not a stand-alone target.
